analysis.one_liner: Repeals the entire Affordable Care Act in a single sentence, with no replacement.
analysis.headline: The one-page repeal bill, sponsored by Sen. Jim DeMint with 22 Republican cosponsors, was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, but never received a hearing, debate, or vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act — the law creating guaranteed coverage for people with pre-existing conditions, health insurance subsidies, the Medicaid expansion, and new taxes on high earners and health companies — in a single line of text. It proposed nothing to replace the law's coverage. It was introduced the day after President Obama signed the ACA and died on the Senate calendar without ever being debated.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be concentrated interests: health insurers, freed from the ACA's minimum medical loss ratio requirement (which forces them to spend most premiums on medical care), its coverage mandates, and its annual industry fee; brand-name drug makers, freed from their fee under the law and the requirement to discount drugs for seniors in the Medicare coverage gap; and high-income households, who would no longer owe the ACA's higher Medicare payroll tax and 3.8% surtax on investment income. Larger employers would no longer face penalties for not offering coverage. People with pre-existing conditions, subsidized buyers of insurance, and seniors would lose protections and financial help.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurers, brand-name drug makers, high earners

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and its amendments in full, in a one-line bill with no replacement, as a CRS summary of the bill confirms.

Repeal would free health insurers from the law's minimum medical loss ratio rule (which caps the share of premiums they can keep for overhead and profit), its required benefit mandates, and the law's annual fee on the insurance industry — while also taking away the millions of subsidized customers the law directed to them.

Repeal would end the ACA's taxes and fees aimed at concentrated interests, including the industry fees and the higher Medicare payroll tax and 3.8% investment-income surtax on households above roughly $200,000–$250,000, and would remove the employer-mandate penalties on larger firms.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people with the most at stake: the millions with pre-existing conditions would again be denied coverage or charged unaffordable prices; the newly subsidized individual-market customers and the states slated for the 2014 Medicaid expansion would lose that help; seniors would pay more as drug discounts and donut-hole relief disappeared; young adults would lose the ability to stay on a parent's plan; and small-business tax credits would vanish. Because the bill contained no replacement, all of this would be lost at once.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions, uninsured families, seniors

drawbacks.text: The bill was a single sentence repealing the entire law with no replacement, so it would have stripped away not only the provisions Republicans opposed but also provisions with broad support — guaranteed coverage regardless of pre-existing conditions, dependent coverage for young adults, and closing the Medicare drug-coverage gap — leaving the health system with no plan for what came next.

Repeal would have removed federal help that reduced uninsured rates and out-of-pocket costs, including premium subsidies and the Medicaid expansion scheduled to begin in 2014, shifting those costs back onto families, hospitals that provide uncompensated care, and state budgets.

A supporter's honest case was that the ACA's mandates, taxes, and penalties burdened employers and middle-class households who faced penalties for going without coverage; this bill answered that by repeal alone rather than by targeted reform.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains went mainly to insurers, drug makers, and high earners, while its costs — loss of guaranteed coverage, subsidies, and senior drug discounts — fell on ordinary people, all without any replacement plan. For most readers, the drawbacks outweighed the benefits; the main population that clearly stood to gain financially was households paying the ACA's investment-income surtax.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced the day after the ACA was signed, it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, but no committee ever took it up and no vote was ever held before the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim DeMint introduced the bill on March 23, 2010 — the same day President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act into law — joined by 12 other Senate Republicans as original cosponsors.

The Senate read the bill twice and placed it on the legislative calendar under General Orders on the day of introduction; that step puts a bill in the queue for possible floor action but guarantees nothing.

The full action history shows nothing after the calendar placement: no committee assignment, no hearing, no floor debate, and no vote. Twenty-two of the Senate's 40 Republicans cosponsored, but the Democratic majority that controlled the Senate never brought it up.
The bill died on the calendar when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the Affordable Care Act remained law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who had gained protections under the new law — those with pre-existing conditions, subsidized insurance buyers, and seniors getting drug discounts — kept them, because the repeal never advanced. The bill served its sponsors mainly as a public record of opposition rather than as a serious legislative vehicle.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ACA beneficiaries; the repeal never advanced

for.name: Jim DeMint
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the day the ACA was signed

against.name: Senate Democratic majority
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it never received a hearing, floor debate, or vote and died on the calendar

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans — 23 of the Senate's 40 — with no Democratic support; no vote was ever held, so the split was reflected in sponsorship rather than roll calls.

industries.note: Repeal would have freed insurers from the ACA's medical loss ratio rule, coverage mandates, and industry fee, but also stripped away the mandate and subsidies that steer millions of paying customers to them. Whatever the industry balance, repeal would have taken guaranteed-coverage protections away from the public.

Repeal would have ended the industry's annual ACA fee and the required 50% discount brand drugs give seniors in the Medicare coverage gap, raising drug costs for seniors. (It would also have erased the law's biosimilar pathway, a further gain for incumbents.)

Repeal would have eliminated the ACA's higher Medicare payroll tax and its 3.8% surtax on investment income for households over roughly $200,000–$250,000, a direct tax cut for the wealthiest households.

Repeal would have removed the ACA's penalties on large employers that do not offer affordable coverage, though employers would also have faced rising uncompensated-care and cost-shifting pressures as more people lost insurance.
